specStatements.text: Metals react with oxygen to produce metal oxides. The reactions are oxidation reactions because the metals gain oxygen.
Students should be able to explain reduction and oxidation in terms of loss or gain of oxygen.

When metals react with other substances the metal atoms form positive ions. The reactivity of a metal is related to its tendency to form positive ions. Metals can be arranged in order of their reactivity in a reactivity series. The metals potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron and copper can be put in order of their reactivity from their reactions with water and dilute acids.
The non-metals hydrogen and carbon are often included in the reactivity series.
A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a compound.
Students should be able to:

recall and describe the reactions, if any, of potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron and copper with water or dilute acids and where appropriate, to place these metals in order of reactivity
explain how the reactivity of metals with water or dilute acids is related to the tendency of the metal to form its positive ion
deduce an order of reactivity of metals based on experimental results.
The reactions of metals with water and acids are limited to room temperature and do not include reactions with steam.
Unreactive metals such as gold are found in the Earth as the metal itself but most metals are found as compounds that require chemical reactions to extract the metal.
Metals less reactive than carbon can be extracted from their oxides by reduction with carbon.
Reduction involves the loss of oxygen.
Knowledge and understanding are limited to the reduction of oxides using carbon.
Knowledge of the details of processes used in the extraction of metals is not required.
Students should be able to:
interpret or evaluate specific metal extraction processes when given appropriate information
identify the substances which are oxidised or reduced in terms of gain or loss of oxygen.
Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons.
write ionic equations for displacement reactions
identify in a given reaction, symbol equation or half equation which species are oxidised and which are reduced.

scopeNotes.statement: The reactions of metals with water and acids are limited to room temperature and do not include reactions with steam.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every reaction with water described in this content is a reaction with cold water at room temperature, and every acid reaction is with dilute acid at room temperature. Magnesium is therefore described as reacting only very slowly with cold water; the vigorous magnesium-steam reaction is named once, in the correction to a misconception, purely to tell students it lies outside what they are required to know. No item asks for observations, products or equations for any metal with steam, and no item requires heating a metal with water.

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge and understanding are limited to the reduction of oxides using carbon.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The only extraction chemistry taught here is the reduction of a metal oxide by carbon, and every extraction equation used is an oxide plus carbon. No item asks students to extract a metal from a sulfide, a carbonate or a halide, and no item requires the reduction of an oxide by hydrogen, by carbon monoxide or by any other reducing agent. Where a metal above carbon is discussed, students are asked only to conclude that carbon cannot be used; the method that is actually used for such metals is not taught or tested here.

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge of the details of processes used in the extraction of metals is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item requires recall of the blast furnace, of electrolysis cells, of smelting conditions, of ore concentration, or of any industrial plant or its economics. Where an extraction process appears, all the information needed is supplied in the stem, and the student is asked only to interpret or evaluate that supplied information against the reactivity series, which is what the specification's skill statement asks for.

concepts.definition: A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen. When a metal reacts with oxygen the metal gains oxygen, so the metal is oxidised.
The compound formed when a metal reacts with oxygen, for example magnesium oxide from magnesium and copper(II) oxide from copper. It contains the metal combined with oxygen, not simply mixed with it.
A reaction in which a substance loses oxygen. When a metal oxide loses its oxygen the metal oxide is reduced.

concepts.term: Formation of positive ions by metals
concepts.definition: When metals react with other substances the metal atoms form positive ions, for example magnesium atoms forming Mg2+ ions.
Metals arranged in order of their reactivity. The order for the metals named in the specification, most reactive first, is potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, copper.

concepts.term: Reaction of a metal with water
concepts.definition: At room temperature potassium, sodium, lithium and calcium react with water to give a metal hydroxide and hydrogen; magnesium reacts only very slowly; zinc, iron and copper show no reaction. Potassium is the most vigorous, then sodium, then lithium, then calcium.

concepts.term: Reaction of a metal with dilute acid
concepts.definition: A metal that reacts with dilute acid gives a salt and hydrogen, seen as fizzing. Calcium reacts very vigorously, magnesium rapidly, zinc more slowly, iron slowly, and copper not at all. Potassium, sodium and lithium react dangerously fast and are not used with acid in a school laboratory.

concepts.term: Carbon and hydrogen in the reactivity series
concepts.definition: The non-metals hydrogen and carbon are often included in the reactivity series so that their reactivity can be compared with that of the metals. Carbon lies between magnesium and zinc; hydrogen lies between iron and copper.
A reaction in which a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound, for example zinc added to copper(II) sulfate solution giving zinc sulfate and copper.

concepts.term: Reactivity and tendency to form positive ions
concepts.definition: The reactivity of a metal is related to its tendency to form positive ions. A metal that forms its positive ion readily reacts readily with water and with dilute acid; a metal that does not form its ion readily, such as copper, reacts slowly or not at all.

Comparing how fast the same reaction happens for different metals under the same conditions, for example how quickly each fizzes in the same dilute acid, allows the metals to be placed in order of reactivity. The faster the reaction, the more reactive the metal.
A metal found in the Earth as the metal itself rather than as a compound. Gold is found this way because it is so unreactive.
Most metals are found in the Earth combined with other elements as compounds, in rock often called an ore. A chemical reaction is needed to separate the metal from what it is combined with.

Metals less reactive than carbon can be extracted from their oxides by heating the oxide with carbon. The oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced, and the carbon gains that oxygen, so it is oxidised, for example 2CuO + C -> 2Cu + CO2.

concepts.term: Identifying what is oxidised and what is reduced
concepts.definition: In a reaction where oxygen is transferred, the substance that gains oxygen is oxidised and the substance that loses oxygen is reduced. Both happen in the same reaction.
Judging, from information given, whether a stated method of extracting a metal will work, chiefly by comparing the position of the metal with the position of carbon in the reactivity series.
Oxidation is the loss of electrons. A metal atom that forms a positive ion has lost electrons and has been oxidised.
Reduction is the gain of electrons. A positive metal ion that becomes a metal atom has gained electrons and has been reduced.

concepts.term: Ionic equation for a displacement reaction
concepts.definition: An equation showing only the species that change, with the spectator ions left out, for example Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu for zinc added to copper(II) sulfate solution.
An equation showing the electrons lost or gained by one species, for example Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e- for oxidation and Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu for reduction.

misconceptions.question: In the reaction 2CuO + C -> 2Cu + CO2, what does it mean to say the copper oxide is reduced?
misconceptions.correct: The copper oxide loses its oxygen to the carbon.
misconceptions.misconception: Reduced means there is less of it, so the solid must simply have got smaller or lighter.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday English 'reduce' means to make smaller, and the solid in the crucible does lose mass, which seems to confirm it.
misconceptions.correction: In chemistry, reduction has a fixed meaning: loss of oxygen. The mass falls because oxygen has been removed by the carbon, but the falling mass is a consequence, not the definition.

misconceptions.question: Carbon removes the oxygen from zinc oxide. Is anything oxidised in this reaction?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The zinc oxide is reduced and, in the same reaction, the carbon is oxidised because it gains that oxygen.
misconceptions.misconception: A reaction is either an oxidation or a reduction, so if the oxide is reduced then nothing is oxidised.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two words are learned separately, and questions often ask for only one of them, so students treat them as labels for two different reactions.
misconceptions.correction: Oxygen has to go somewhere. Whenever one substance loses oxygen another substance gains it, so reduction and oxidation always happen together in the same reaction.

misconceptions.question: When magnesium reacts, what kind of ion does the magnesium form?
misconceptions.correct: A positive ion, Mg2+.
misconceptions.misconception: Metals form negative ions when they react, because reacting means picking something up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'gaining' with reacting, and the charge signs are easy to swap when the reason for them is not held in mind.
misconceptions.correction: When metals react the metal atoms form positive ions. The reactivity of a metal is related to how readily it forms that positive ion.

misconceptions.question: What happens when copper turnings are left in dilute hydrochloric acid?
misconceptions.correct: Nothing. Copper does not react with dilute acid.
misconceptions.misconception: Copper fizzes slowly with dilute acid, because it is a metal and all metals react with acids.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule 'metal + acid -> salt + hydrogen' is taught as though it applied to every metal, and copper's slow tarnishing in air looks like a slow reaction.
misconceptions.correction: Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids. Copper is below hydrogen, so no reaction happens and no hydrogen is produced.

misconceptions.question: How does magnesium react with cold water?
misconceptions.correct: Very slowly indeed; only a few bubbles appear, even after a long time.
misconceptions.misconception: Magnesium reacts rapidly with cold water and gives off plenty of hydrogen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember magnesium fizzing hard in dilute acid, or the vigorous demonstration in which magnesium is heated in steam, and transfer that to cold water.
misconceptions.correction: At room temperature magnesium reacts with water only very slowly. The vigorous reaction is with steam, which this specification does not require.

misconceptions.question: Which is the most reactive: lithium, sodium or potassium?
misconceptions.correct: Potassium, then sodium, then lithium.
misconceptions.misconception: Lithium is the most reactive because it is the first metal at the top of Group 1.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In many other patterns the top of a group or a list means 'most', and lithium is the alkali metal students meet first.
misconceptions.correction: Reactivity of the alkali metals increases going down the group. The specification lists them potassium, sodium, lithium, in that order of reactivity.

misconceptions.question: Carbon and hydrogen appear in the reactivity series. What does that tell you about them?
misconceptions.correct: Nothing about their classification; they are non-metals, placed there so their reactivity can be compared with the metals.
misconceptions.misconception: They must be metals, otherwise they would not be in a series of metals.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The series is introduced as 'the reactivity series of metals', so anything in it is assumed to be a metal.
misconceptions.correction: The non-metals hydrogen and carbon are often included in the reactivity series. Their position is a useful comparison; it does not make them metals.

misconceptions.question: Will copper displace magnesium from magnesium sulfate solution?
misconceptions.correct: No. Copper is less reactive than magnesium, so no displacement happens.
misconceptions.misconception: Any metal will displace any other metal from its compound if it is left long enough or heated.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Displacement is first met as a reaction that 'happens', so students learn the event rather than the condition that allows it.
misconceptions.correction: Only a more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a compound. If the added metal is the less reactive one, there is no reaction at all.

misconceptions.question: Zinc is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. Which metal ends up in the solution?
misconceptions.correct: Zinc, as zinc ions. The copper leaves the solution and forms as solid copper.
misconceptions.misconception: Copper ends up in solution, because the copper was in the compound to start with and it pushes the zinc out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read the compound as the active partner because it is written first, and the direction of the swap is easy to reverse.
misconceptions.correction: The more reactive metal takes the place in the compound. Zinc is more reactive, so zinc goes into solution and copper comes out as the metal.

misconceptions.question: Why is gold found in the Earth as the metal itself?
misconceptions.correct: Because gold is so unreactive that it does not form compounds with the substances around it.
misconceptions.misconception: Because gold is rare, so there is too little of it to react with anything.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rarity and value are the facts about gold that students already know, so they are reached for first when a reason is wanted.
misconceptions.correction: How much of an element there is has nothing to do with whether it reacts. Unreactive metals such as gold are found as the metal itself; most metals are found as compounds.

misconceptions.question: Can carbon be used to extract any metal from its oxide?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only metals less reactive than carbon can be extracted from their oxides by reduction with carbon.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon works for every metal, because carbon burns so readily and takes oxygen from anything.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon reduction is the only extraction method taught in this part of the specification, so it is assumed to be universal.
misconceptions.correction: Carbon can only take the oxygen from the oxides of metals below it in the reactivity series. Metals above carbon, such as magnesium, cannot be extracted this way.

misconceptions.question: In the reduction of copper(II) oxide with carbon, which substance is reduced?
misconceptions.correct: The copper(II) oxide, because it is the substance that loses oxygen.
misconceptions.misconception: The carbon is reduced, because the process is called reduction with carbon and carbon is the thing doing it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name of the process puts 'reduction' next to 'carbon', and the substance that causes a change is assumed to be the one described by the change.
misconceptions.correction: Carbon is the reducing agent: it causes the reduction of the oxide by taking its oxygen. Carbon itself gains oxygen, so carbon is oxidised.

misconceptions.question: In 2Fe2O3 + 3C -> 4Fe + 3CO2, is the iron oxidised?
misconceptions.correct: No. The iron oxide is reduced, because it loses oxygen. The carbon is oxidised.
misconceptions.misconception: The iron is oxidised, because a fresh metal is produced and metals are the things that get oxidised.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Nearly every earlier example of oxidation involved a metal gaining oxygen, so 'metal' and 'oxidised' become linked in students' minds.
misconceptions.correction: Judge each substance by what happens to its oxygen. Here the iron oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced; only the carbon gains oxygen, so only the carbon is oxidised.

misconceptions.question: In terms of electrons, what is oxidation?
misconceptions.correct: The loss of electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Oxidation is gaining electrons, because oxidation is gaining oxygen so it must be gaining something else too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The oxygen definition is learned as 'gain', so the electron definition is assumed to be a gain as well; the two definitions do run opposite ways.
misconceptions.correction: Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons. A metal atom forming a positive ion has lost electrons, so it has been oxidised.

misconceptions.question: Zinc is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. What is the ionic equation?
misconceptions.correct: Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu.
misconceptions.misconception: The ionic equation is Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu, because that shows all the substances present.
misconceptions.whyItArises: It is the equation students already know for the reaction, and leaving out a substance that is genuinely in the beaker feels like leaving out part of the answer.
misconceptions.correction: An ionic equation shows only the species that change. The sulfate ions are unchanged spectator ions, so they are left out.

misconceptions.question: A species changes from Mg to Mg2+. Has it been oxidised or reduced?
misconceptions.correct: Oxidised, because it has lost two electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Reduced, because its charge has gone up, and going up means it has gained something.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Gained' is attached to the number getting bigger rather than to the electrons, and the charge rises precisely because electrons are lost.
misconceptions.correction: Track the electrons, not the sign of the charge. Losing negative electrons makes the charge more positive, and loss of electrons is oxidation.

misconceptions.question: What gas bubbles off when magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid?
misconceptions.correct: Hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Oxygen, because bubbles of gas in a liquid are usually oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oxygen is the gas students name most readily, and bubbles in water are met first in photosynthesis experiments where the gas really is oxygen.
misconceptions.correction: A metal reacting with a dilute acid gives a salt and hydrogen. The hydrogen comes from the acid; no oxygen is produced.

misconceptions.question: What are the products when sodium reacts with water?
misconceptions.correct: Sodium hydroxide and hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Sodium oxide and hydrogen, because the water supplies the oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Metal + oxygen -> metal oxide is learned just beforehand, and water does contain oxygen, so the oxide is assumed.
misconceptions.correction: A metal reacting with water gives a metal hydroxide and hydrogen: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2. The resulting solution is alkaline.

misconceptions.question: Magnesium is above carbon in the reactivity series. What does that mean for extracting magnesium?
misconceptions.correct: It means carbon cannot be used to extract it; a different method is needed, which this part of the specification does not cover.
misconceptions.misconception: It means magnesium cannot be extracted from its ore at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon reduction is the only method taught here, so 'carbon will not work' is heard as 'nothing will work'.
misconceptions.correction: Metals more reactive than carbon are extracted by another method. The specification limits knowledge here to the reduction of oxides using carbon, so only the conclusion 'carbon cannot be used' is required.

misconceptions.question: Metal P bubbles very fast for 20 seconds; metal Q bubbles slowly for five minutes. Which is more reactive?
misconceptions.correct: P, because it reacts faster under the same conditions.
misconceptions.misconception: Q, because it keeps producing gas for much longer, so it gives more gas in total.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Total gas produced depends on how much metal was used, but students read a long-lasting reaction as a strong one.
misconceptions.correction: Reactivity is judged by the rate of reaction under the same conditions, not by the total volume of gas. The total depends on the amount of metal, not on how reactive it is.

misconceptions.question: Which is more reactive, lithium or calcium?
misconceptions.correct: Lithium. The specification's order is potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium.
misconceptions.misconception: Calcium, because calcium fizzes harder in cold water than a small piece of lithium does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Calcium releases hydrogen quickly and the mixture turns cloudy, which looks more dramatic than lithium quietly fizzing on the surface.
misconceptions.correction: One demonstration is not a controlled comparison. In the reactivity series the specification gives, lithium is placed above calcium.

misconceptions.question: Magnesium burns in air. What has happened to the magnesium atoms?
misconceptions.correct: They have combined with oxygen, forming magnesium ions in the compound magnesium oxide.
misconceptions.misconception: They are still magnesium atoms; the oxygen has just got mixed in among them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The white powder still contains magnesium, and the difference between a mixture and a compound is easy to lose sight of when a solid simply changes colour.
misconceptions.correction: A new substance has been made. The metal atoms form positive ions and are held to oxygen in a compound, which cannot be separated by physical means.

misconceptions.question: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen.
misconceptions.correct: Oxidation is gain of oxygen; reduction is loss of oxygen.
misconceptions.misconception: Oxidation is loss of oxygen and reduction is gain of oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two definitions are learned as a pair and are easy to attach the wrong way round, especially as 'reduction' sounds like something being taken away from the reactant that is named.
misconceptions.correction: Fix it on the word: oxidation adds oxygen. So the substance that gains oxygen is oxidised, and the substance that loses oxygen is reduced.

misconceptions.question: Sodium is soft and floats. Is that why it is so reactive?
misconceptions.correct: No. Its reactivity comes from how readily its atoms form positive ions.
misconceptions.misconception: A metal that is soft, light or low-melting is reactive; a hard, dense metal is unreactive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The reactive metals students meet happen to be soft and low-density, so the physical property is mistaken for the cause.
misconceptions.correction: Physical properties do not decide chemical reactivity. The reactivity of a metal is related to its tendency to form positive ions.

misconceptions.question: A metal produces no bubbles at all in dilute acid. What does that show?
misconceptions.correct: That it does not react with the acid, so it is the least reactive metal tested.
misconceptions.misconception: That it reacted so fast it finished before you could see it, so it is the most reactive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know a very fast reaction can be over quickly, and 'nothing to see' is read as 'already over' rather than 'nothing happened'.
misconceptions.correction: No bubbles at any point means no hydrogen was produced and no reaction took place. Copper behaves this way with dilute acid.

misconceptions.question: Zinc is dipped into copper(II) sulfate and becomes coated with copper. Which metal is more reactive?
misconceptions.correct: Zinc, because it displaced the copper from the compound.
misconceptions.misconception: Copper, because copper is the metal that came out and settled on top.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The copper coating is the visible product, and students read 'the metal that appears' as 'the metal that won'.
misconceptions.correction: The metal that appears as a solid is the one that has been pushed out of its compound, so it is the less reactive one. Zinc went into solution, so zinc is more reactive.

misconceptions.question: Iron is found in the Earth combined with oxygen. Could it be separated by crushing and sieving the rock?
misconceptions.correct: No. Iron and oxygen are chemically combined, so a chemical reaction is needed.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes, because the rock is a mixture of iron and other stuff, so sorting the pieces would separate it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rock does look like a mixture of bits, and students apply the separation techniques they know for mixtures to a compound.
misconceptions.correction: Most metals are found as compounds that require chemical reactions to extract the metal. Physical separation cannot break the bonds in a compound.

misconceptions.question: Copper is well below carbon in the reactivity series. Can carbon reduce copper(II) oxide?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Any metal less reactive than carbon can be extracted from its oxide with carbon.
misconceptions.misconception: No, copper is far too unreactive for carbon to do anything to its oxide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know that being unreactive stops a metal reacting, and apply that to the oxide, which is the substance actually being attacked here.
misconceptions.correction: It is the metal's oxide that reacts with carbon, and the less reactive the metal, the more easily its oxide gives up oxygen. Being below carbon is exactly the condition needed.

misconceptions.question: Is CuO + C -> Cu + CO2 an acceptable equation for this extraction?
misconceptions.correct: No. The oxygen atoms do not balance, so the equation is wrong.
misconceptions.misconception: It is fine, because it shows the right reactants and the right products.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students check that the substances are correct and treat the balancing numbers as decoration rather than as part of the chemistry.
misconceptions.correction: Every atom must be accounted for. Two oxygen atoms are needed on the right, so two copper oxides are needed on the left: 2CuO + C -> 2Cu + CO2.

misconceptions.question: How does a magnesium atom become a magnesium ion?
misconceptions.correct: By losing two electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: By gaining two protons, since protons carry the positive charge.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The charge is positive and protons are the positive particles, so students change the protons rather than the electrons.
misconceptions.correction: The number of protons fixes which element it is and never changes in a chemical reaction. Charge is changed by losing or gaining electrons.

misconceptions.question: What is the charge on a zinc ion in an ionic equation?
misconceptions.correct: 2+, so the ion is written Zn2+.
misconceptions.misconception: 1+, because metal ions carry a single positive charge.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sodium and potassium ions are met first and both are 1+, so a single positive charge is taken as the standard for metals.
misconceptions.correction: The charge must make the equation balance for charge as well as atoms. Zinc forms Zn2+, so Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu balances at 2+ on each side.

mcqs.stem: Zinc powder is heated strongly in air and turns into a white solid. Which statement about the zinc is correct?

options.text: Zinc loses mass, so the zinc is reduced.
options.rationale: A student who reads 'reduced' as 'made smaller' looks for a loss, and mistakes the everyday meaning of the word for the chemical one.

options.text: Oxygen gains zinc, so the oxygen is oxidised.
options.rationale: Reverses which substance the definition is applied to; the student sees a combination and labels whichever substance is named second.

options.text: Zinc gains oxygen, so the zinc is oxidised.
options.rationale: Metals react with oxygen to produce metal oxides, and the reaction is an oxidation because the metal gains oxygen.

options.text: Zinc and oxygen mix, so neither is changed.
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who treats the white solid as zinc with oxygen mixed in rather than as a new compound.

mcqs.stem: Copper turns black when heated in air: 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO. Why is the copper said to be oxidised?

options.text: The copper has gained oxygen.
options.rationale: Oxidation in terms of oxygen means gain of oxygen, and the copper has combined with oxygen to form copper(II) oxide.

options.text: The copper has lost some mass.
options.rationale: Comes from the everyday sense of 'reduce' and 'oxidise' as getting smaller or bigger, rather than from oxygen transfer. The copper in fact gains mass.

options.text: The copper has lost oxygen.
options.rationale: The two oxygen definitions have been attached the wrong way round; this describes reduction, not oxidation.

options.text: The copper has changed colour.
options.rationale: A student who identifies oxidation by its appearance picks the observation rather than the chemistry; the colour change is evidence, not the definition.

mcqs.stem: Zinc oxide is heated with carbon: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. Which substance is reduced?

options.text: Zinc oxide, because it loses oxygen
options.rationale: The zinc oxide gives up its oxygen and becomes zinc, and loss of oxygen is reduction.

options.text: Carbon, because it reduces the oxide
options.rationale: Confuses the substance that causes the reduction with the substance that is reduced; carbon takes the oxygen, so carbon is oxidised.

options.text: Carbon, because it gains some oxygen
options.rationale: Correctly spots that carbon gains oxygen but applies the wrong label to it; gaining oxygen is oxidation.

options.text: Carbon monoxide, because it forms
options.rationale: Picks the new product rather than tracking oxygen; being formed in a reaction does not make a substance reduced.

mcqs.stem: When a metal reacts with another substance, what happens to the metal atoms?

options.text: They become negative ions.
options.rationale: The charge is remembered but its sign is reversed; students who link 'reacting' with 'gaining' choose the negative ion.

options.text: They form positive ions.
options.rationale: When metals react with other substances the metal atoms form positive ions, and the reactivity of a metal is related to that tendency.

options.text: They stay as neutral atoms.
options.rationale: Comes from treating a reaction as a mixing together rather than as a chemical change in which ions are formed.

options.text: They form small molecules.
options.rationale: Transfers bonding in non-metals to metals; metal atoms in compounds are present as positive ions, not as molecules.

mcqs.stem: Which list places these metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first?

options.text: lithium, sodium, magnesium, copper
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who assumes the first alkali metal in the group is the most reactive; reactivity in fact increases down Group 1.

options.text: sodium, lithium, copper, magnesium
options.rationale: Places copper above magnesium, which a student does if they believe copper reacts with dilute acids like other metals.

options.text: sodium, lithium, magnesium, copper
options.rationale: This is the order given in the specification: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, copper.

options.text: magnesium, sodium, lithium, copper
options.rationale: Puts magnesium first because its burning in air is the most memorable demonstration; brightness of burning is not the test used here.

mcqs.stem: Why are the non-metals carbon and hydrogen often included in the reactivity series?

options.text: They are counted as metals in the series.
options.rationale: Assumes anything in a series of metals must be a metal; carbon and hydrogen are non-metals whatever their position.

options.text: They react with all metals in the series.
options.rationale: Follows from believing carbon attacks every metal compound; position in the series shows a comparison, not a guarantee of reaction.

options.text: They are made whenever a metal reacts.
options.rationale: Overgeneralises from metal and acid reactions, where hydrogen is a product; carbon is not produced in these reactions at all.

options.text: Their reactivity can be compared with metals.
options.rationale: Including them lets their position be used to predict, for example, whether carbon will take oxygen from a metal oxide.

mcqs.stem: Iron filings are stirred into copper(II) sulfate solution. What happens, and why?

options.text: Copper forms, as iron is more reactive.
options.rationale: A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a compound; iron is above copper, so iron takes its place and copper is released.

options.text: Iron forms, as copper pushes out the iron.
options.rationale: Reverses the direction of displacement, treating the metal already in the compound as the one that does the pushing.

options.text: Copper forms, as any metal displaces another.
options.rationale: Reaches the right observation by the wrong rule; displacement only happens when the added metal is the more reactive one.

options.text: No change, as both metals are unreactive.
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who judges both metals to be 'not very reactive' and so predicts nothing; iron is above copper, so a reaction occurs.

mcqs.stem: Small pieces of four metals are each dropped into cold water at room temperature. Which reacts most vigorously?

options.text: Lithium
options.rationale: Chosen by students who place lithium at the top of Group 1 for reactivity; lithium fizzes steadily but far less vigorously than potassium.

options.text: Magnesium
options.rationale: Chosen by students recalling magnesium's vigorous fizzing in acid or in steam; with cold water magnesium reacts only very slowly.

options.text: Copper
options.rationale: Picked by students who take the green coating on old copper as evidence of a fast reaction with water; copper does not react with water.

options.text: Potassium
options.rationale: Potassium is the most reactive metal in the specification's list and reacts violently with cold water, the hydrogen burning with a lilac flame.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. What are the products?

options.text: Magnesium chloride and oxygen
options.rationale: The salt is right but the gas is not; oxygen is the gas students name most readily when they see bubbles.

options.text: Magnesium oxide and hydrogen
options.rationale: Applies metal + oxygen -> metal oxide to an acid reaction; the metal combines with the chloride from the acid, not with oxygen.

options.text: Magnesium hydroxide and chlorine
options.rationale: Mixes up the water reaction, which gives a hydroxide, with the acid reaction, and releases the acid's chlorine as a gas.

options.text: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen
options.rationale: A metal reacting with a dilute acid gives a salt and hydrogen: Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2.

mcqs.stem: Copper turnings are left in dilute sulfuric acid for an hour. What is seen?

options.text: Slow fizzing; copper reacts with all acids.
options.rationale: Applies metal + acid -> salt + hydrogen to every metal without checking the metal's position relative to hydrogen.

options.text: Oxygen bubbles form on the copper surface.
options.rationale: Names the wrong gas as well as predicting a reaction; the gas from a metal and an acid is hydrogen, and here there is no gas at all.

options.text: No reaction; copper is below hydrogen.
options.rationale: Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids, so copper gives no reaction and no gas.

options.text: The copper dissolves into a blue solution.
options.rationale: Copper(II) sulfate solution is blue and familiar, so students expect it to appear; it cannot form here because no reaction occurs.

mcqs.stem: Why does potassium react far more vigorously with water than iron does?

options.text: Potassium gains electrons more readily than iron.
options.rationale: Has the right idea that electrons are involved but the wrong direction; metal atoms lose electrons to form positive ions.

options.text: Potassium is much softer and less dense than iron.
options.rationale: Substitutes a physical property for a chemical explanation; softness and density do not determine reactivity.

options.text: Potassium forms its positive ion far more readily.
options.rationale: The reactivity of a metal is related to its tendency to form positive ions, and potassium forms K+ much more readily than iron forms its ion.

options.text: Iron is protected by a layer of rust on its surface.
options.rationale: Offers a barrier explanation instead of the metal's own chemistry; clean iron still does not react with cold water.

mcqs.stem: A student writes: 'The more reactive a metal is, the harder it is for its atoms to form ions.' Why is this wrong?

options.text: Reactive metals form their positive ions most readily.
options.rationale: The reactivity of a metal is related to its tendency to form positive ions, so a high tendency means high reactivity, not the reverse.

options.text: Reactive metals form negative ions, not positive ones.
options.rationale: Corrects the statement in the wrong way, keeping the sign error; when metals react, the metal atoms form positive ions.

options.text: Reactivity depends on the acid used, not on the metal.
options.rationale: Moves the explanation to the other reactant; the same order of reactivity is found with water and with dilute acids.

options.text: Reactivity depends on how hard and dense a metal is.
options.rationale: Replaces the ion explanation with a physical one, which is the commonest wrong answer to 'why is this metal reactive'.

mcqs.stem: Four metals are added to identical samples of dilute acid. P bubbles very fast for 20 s, Q bubbles slowly for 5 minutes, R gives no bubbles, S bubbles steadily for 1 minute. Which metal is most reactive?

options.text: Q, because it bubbles for the longest.
options.rationale: Confuses the total amount of gas with the rate; how long it lasts depends on how much metal was used, not on reactivity.

options.text: P, because it bubbles fastest of all.
options.rationale: Under the same conditions, the faster the reaction, the more reactive the metal, so the fastest fizzing identifies the most reactive metal.

options.text: R, because it was used up instantly.
options.rationale: Reads 'no bubbles' as 'the reaction was over before I looked'; no bubbles at any point means no reaction happened.

options.text: S, because it bubbles at a steady rate.
options.rationale: Treats a controlled, even reaction as the sign of a strong one; steadiness says nothing about how reactive the metal is.

mcqs.stem: A student finds that magnesium displaces zinc from zinc sulfate, and that zinc displaces iron from iron(II) sulfate. What is the order of reactivity, most reactive first?

options.text: iron, zinc, magnesium
options.rationale: Reverses every result by treating the metal in the compound as the one doing the displacing.

options.text: magnesium, iron, zinc
options.rationale: Reverses the second result only, because the iron appears as a solid coating and the student reads the solid that forms as the more reactive metal.

options.text: zinc, magnesium, iron
options.rationale: Puts zinc first because it is the metal named in both results, mistaking how often a metal appears for how reactive it is.

options.text: magnesium, zinc, iron
options.rationale: Each displacement shows the added metal is more reactive than the one in the compound, so magnesium is above zinc and zinc is above iron.

mcqs.stem: Why is gold found in the Earth as the metal itself rather than as a compound?

options.text: Gold is very unreactive, so it stays uncombined.
options.rationale: Unreactive metals such as gold are found in the Earth as the metal itself, because they do not react to form compounds.

options.text: Gold is rare, so there is too little of it to react.
options.rationale: Substitutes rarity for chemistry; how much of an element exists has no bearing on whether it forms compounds.

options.text: Gold compounds are broken apart by sunlight.
options.rationale: Invents a decomposition route rather than accepting that the compounds never form; nothing in the reactivity series supports it.

options.text: Gold is very dense, so it sinks below the ores.
options.rationale: Uses a physical property to explain a chemical fact, which is the commonest way students go wrong on reactivity.

mcqs.stem: Most metals are found in the Earth as compounds. What is needed to obtain the metal itself?

options.text: It is sieved out, since rock is just a mixture.
options.rationale: Applies techniques for separating mixtures to a compound; the metal is chemically combined and cannot be sorted out physically.

options.text: The rock is melted and the metal is poured off.
options.rationale: Assumes melting separates the metal, as it would from a mixture of solids; melting a compound does not release the element.

options.text: Carbon is used to extract all metals from ore.
options.rationale: Takes the one extraction method taught here as universal; carbon only works for metals less reactive than carbon.

options.text: A chemical reaction is needed to release it.
options.rationale: Most metals are found as compounds that require chemical reactions to extract the metal from what it is combined with.

mcqs.stem: Part of the reactivity series is: magnesium, carbon, zinc, iron, copper. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Magnesium oxide is also reduced by carbon.
options.rationale: Ignores the condition on the rule; magnesium is above carbon, so carbon cannot take the oxygen from magnesium oxide.

options.text: Zinc oxide can be reduced to zinc using carbon.
options.rationale: Zinc is less reactive than carbon, and metals less reactive than carbon can be extracted from their oxides by reduction with carbon.

options.text: Copper oxide is too unreactive for carbon.
options.rationale: Assumes a very unreactive metal is beyond reach; being far below carbon is exactly what makes copper oxide easy to reduce.

options.text: Carbon is reduced when it removes the oxygen.
options.rationale: Confuses the reducing agent with the substance reduced; carbon gains the oxygen, so carbon is oxidised.

mcqs.stem: Which equation correctly represents the extraction of copper from copper(II) oxide using carbon?

options.text: CuO + C -> Cu + CO2
options.rationale: Has the right substances but only one oxygen on the left and two on the right, so the equation is not balanced.

options.text: 2CuO + C -> 2Cu + CO2
options.rationale: Balanced for every element: two copper and two oxygen on each side, one carbon on each side, with the oxide reduced and the carbon oxidised.

options.text: 2Cu + CO2 -> 2CuO + C
options.rationale: Written the wrong way round, so the copper gains oxygen; this is the opposite of extracting the metal.

options.text: CuCO3 -> CuO + CO2
options.rationale: A balanced equation the student has met before, but it is the decomposition of copper carbonate and involves no carbon reduction.

mcqs.stem: In terms of oxygen, what does reduction mean?

options.text: A fall in the mass of a substance.
options.rationale: Takes the everyday meaning of 'reduce'; the mass does fall when oxygen leaves, but that is a consequence, not the definition.

options.text: The loss of oxygen from a substance.
options.rationale: Reduction involves the loss of oxygen, which is how metal oxides are turned into metals in extraction.

options.text: The gain of oxygen by a substance.
options.rationale: The definitions of oxidation and reduction have been swapped, which is the commonest error on this pair of terms.

options.text: The breaking down of a substance.
options.rationale: Confuses reduction with decomposition; reduction is specifically the loss of oxygen, not any breakdown.

mcqs.stem: A firm plans to extract tin by heating tin oxide with carbon. It is given that tin lies between iron and copper in the reactivity series. Is the plan sound?

options.text: No, because tin is far too unreactive to react.
options.rationale: Treats low reactivity as a barrier; a metal below carbon is precisely the case where carbon reduction works.

options.text: No, because tin oxide can never be broken down.
options.rationale: Concludes that a metal cannot be obtained at all; the information given shows carbon reduction is available for tin.

options.text: Yes, because carbon can extract any known metal.
options.rationale: Reaches the right verdict by an unsound rule; the position of the metal relative to carbon is what decides it.

options.text: Yes, because tin is less reactive than carbon.
options.rationale: Tin lies below iron, and therefore below carbon, so its oxide can be reduced with carbon exactly as iron and copper oxides can.

mcqs.stem: In a furnace, a metal oxide is heated with carbon and molten metal collects at the bottom. Which conclusion does this support?

options.text: The carbon has been reduced by the oxide.
options.rationale: Reverses the roles; the oxide loses oxygen so the oxide is reduced, while the carbon gains oxygen and is oxidised.

options.text: The metal cannot be extracted in this way.
options.rationale: Contradicts the evidence given, and reflects a belief that carbon reduction rarely works.

options.text: The carbon is only a fuel used for heating.
options.rationale: Carbon does burn to supply heat, but here it also removes the oxygen, which is why the metal is produced.

options.text: The metal is less reactive than carbon.
options.rationale: Carbon has succeeded in taking the oxygen from the oxide, which happens only for metals less reactive than carbon.

mcqs.stem: In the reaction 2Fe2O3 + 3C -> 4Fe + 3CO2, which substance is oxidised?

options.text: iron, because a new metal forms
options.rationale: Links 'metal' with 'oxidised' out of habit; here the iron is released from its oxide rather than combining with oxygen.

options.text: iron oxide, as it loses oxygen
options.rationale: Identifies the oxygen change correctly but labels it the wrong way round; losing oxygen is reduction.

options.text: carbon, because it gains oxygen
options.rationale: The carbon ends up combined with oxygen as carbon dioxide, and gain of oxygen is oxidation.

options.text: carbon dioxide, as it has oxygen
options.rationale: Chooses the product with the most oxygen in it rather than tracking the change; the carbon dioxide is the result, not the substance changed.

mcqs.stem: Zinc oxide is heated with carbon: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Only the zinc oxide changes; it is reduced.
options.rationale: Treats a reaction as either an oxidation or a reduction; oxygen has to be gained by something, so both occur.

options.text: Zinc oxide is oxidised and carbon reduced.
options.rationale: The two labels are attached the wrong way round, which is the commonest error with these definitions.

options.text: Zinc oxide is reduced and carbon is oxidised.
options.rationale: The zinc oxide loses oxygen so it is reduced, and the carbon gains that oxygen so it is oxidised; both happen together.

options.text: Carbon is reduced because its mass falls.
options.rationale: Uses the everyday sense of 'reduced' as getting smaller, instead of the chemical definition of losing oxygen.

mcqs.stem: In terms of electrons, what is oxidation?

options.text: the gain of electrons
options.rationale: The two definitions are swapped, usually because 'oxidation is gain of oxygen' is carried across to electrons.

options.text: the loss of protons
options.rationale: Changes the wrong particle; protons are fixed in a chemical reaction and only electrons are transferred.

options.text: the loss of electrons
options.rationale: Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons.

options.text: the sharing of electrons
options.rationale: Describes covalent bonding rather than a redox change; oxidation involves electrons being lost, not shared.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium reacts with copper(II) ions: Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu. What happens to the magnesium?

options.text: It loses electrons, so it is oxidised.
options.rationale: The magnesium atom becomes Mg2+ by losing two electrons, and loss of electrons is oxidation.

options.text: It gains electrons, so it is oxidised.
options.rationale: Reaches the right label by the wrong route; electrons are lost, not gained, when a metal forms a positive ion.

options.text: It loses electrons, so it is reduced.
options.rationale: Tracks the electrons correctly but names the process wrongly, often because the charge going up is read as a gain.

options.text: It gains protons, so it is oxidised.
options.rationale: Attributes the positive charge to added protons; the proton number never changes in a chemical reaction.

mcqs.stem: Zinc is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. Which is the correct ionic equation?

options.text: Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu
options.rationale: This is the full equation, not the ionic one; the sulfate ions are spectators and should be left out.

options.text: Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu
options.rationale: Shows only the species that change, and balances for both atoms and charge, with 2+ on each side.

options.text: Zn2+ + Cu -> Zn + Cu2+
options.rationale: Runs the displacement the wrong way, with the less reactive copper displacing zinc from solution.

options.text: Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn+ + Cu
options.rationale: Gives zinc a single positive charge, so the equation no longer balances for charge; zinc forms Zn2+.

mcqs.stem: The full equation is Mg + FeSO4 -> MgSO4 + Fe. Which ionic equation shows the change with spectator ions left out?

options.text: Mg + Fe2+ -> Mg2+ + Fe
options.rationale: The sulfate ions are unchanged, so they are removed, leaving the magnesium losing electrons and the iron(II) ions gaining them.

options.text: Mg + FeSO4 -> MgSO4 + Fe
options.rationale: Simply repeats the full equation; an ionic equation must omit the spectator ions.

options.text: Fe + Mg2+ -> Fe2+ + Mg
options.rationale: Reverses the displacement, so the less reactive iron pushes out magnesium, which does not happen.

options.text: Mg + Fe2+ -> Mg+ + Fe
options.rationale: Uses a 1+ charge for magnesium, leaving the charges unbalanced; magnesium forms Mg2+.

mcqs.stem: Consider the half equation Fe2+ + 2e- -> Fe. What does it show?

options.text: Iron ions are oxidised by gaining electrons.
options.rationale: Reads the electrons correctly but swaps the labels, applying 'gain means oxidation' from the oxygen definition.

options.text: Iron ions are reduced by gaining electrons.
options.rationale: The iron(II) ions take in two electrons each, and gain of electrons is reduction.

options.text: Iron ions are reduced by losing their charge.
options.rationale: Explains it by the charge falling rather than by electrons being gained, which fails on half equations written the other way.

options.text: Iron atoms are oxidised by losing electrons.
options.rationale: Describes the reverse half equation, Fe -> Fe2+ + 2e-, which is not the one written here.

mcqs.stem: In the reaction Mg + Zn2+ -> Mg2+ + Zn, which species is reduced?

options.text: Zn2+, because it gains two electrons.
options.rationale: The zinc ions take two electrons each to become zinc atoms, and gain of electrons is reduction.

options.text: Mg, because its charge increases.
options.rationale: Reads a rise in charge as a gain of something; the charge rises because electrons are lost, which is oxidation.

options.text: Mg, because it loses two electrons.
options.rationale: Correctly identifies the electron loss but calls it reduction; loss of electrons is oxidation.

options.text: Zn, because it forms a solid metal.
options.rationale: Names the product rather than the species that changed; the zinc atoms are the result of the reduction of Zn2+.
